Several repositories in your notebook explicitly measure coding-agent harness modifications, prompt changes, or context-engineering strategies by **end outcomes** (such as benchmark pass rates, unit test resolution, solve rates, or cost per accepted outcome) rather than just proxy metrics like token count savings [1-5]. 

---

### 1. Harness² (`google-research/harness2`)
**Harness²** is a framework dedicated to **recursive agent harnessing** [6]. It treats the agent harness—encompassing prompts, guardrails, tool guidance, subagents, skills, scripts, memory, and plugins [7]—as an editable system optimized through task-level and harnessing-level recursion while keeping model weights fixed [1, 6].

* **Outcome-Based Evaluation & Benchmarks**:
  Harness² measures harness and prompt edits by evaluating end-task outcomes across three professional benchmarks [1, 8]:
  * **WorkBuddy-Bench** (office, web, and code tasks) [8]
  * **JobBench** (professional work tasks) [8]
  * **LAB** (legal work tasks) [8]
  * Evaluated models include GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash [1].

* **Sample Sizes & Recursion Modes**:
  * **Task-Level Recursion Budget (\\(K\\))**: Harness² evaluates scaling task-level recursion in two ways [9]:
    * **Parallel Recursion (`--k K --mode parallel`)**: Probes \\(K\\) general and \\(K\\) domain-specific candidate harnesses on a task and composes refinements from their execution evidence [9].
    * **Sequential Recursion (`--k K --mode sequential`)**: Refines the harness sequentially through \\(K\\) successive Propose–Probe–Compose steps [9].

* **Variance Control & Seeds**:
  * **Seed & Configuration Alignment**: Judging and reporting workflows strictly require using the exact same benchmark, executor, subset, recursion budget (`--k`), mode, and **seed** as the refinement run [8].
  * **Environment Isolation & Contamination Guard**: Evaluator network access is configured prior to evaluation to restrict access to online benchmark rubrics or answers [10].

* **Primary Metrics**:
  * **Benchmark Pass Rate**: Overall accuracy gains (e.g., up to +11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench and +4.5 points on JobBench) [1].
  * **Partial Pass Rate**: Measured specifically on benchmarks like LAB (+11.8 percentage point increase) [1].

---

### 2. Trail-Code (`trailhq/Trail-Code`)
**Trail-Code** evaluates how wiring a codebase "graft map" (a structural code graph built via `tree-sitter`) and session "learnings" into coding agents (e.g., Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) alters task resolution and efficiency [2, 11, 12].

* **Outcome-Based Evaluation & Benchmarks**:
  * **SWE-bench Verified**: Tested on **50 real GitHub issues** graded by the official `swebench` harness using maintainers' actual unit test suites (a binary pass/fail based on flipping failing tests without breaking passing ones) [3, 13].
  * **Internal Controlled Sweep**: Evaluated across **162 runs** on two repositories (including a Node/Express authentication service) [14, 15].
  * **Real Repository Tasks (PocketBase)**: Tested across **15 real tasks** (10 developer questions and 5 actual merged pull requests re-implemented from base commits and scored against files maintainers changed) [16, 17].

* **Sample Sizes & Multi-Trial Setup**:
  * **SWE-bench Verified**: \\(N = 50\\) instances using the same underlying model (**Claude Sonnet 5**), identical Docker containers, and fixed turn limits across cold vs. graft-map arms [3, 13].
  * **Controlled Sweep**: **162 total runs**, running 3 trials per task to account for LLM non-determinism across single-file and multi-file tasks [14, 15].

* **Variance Control & Scoring Judges**:
  * **SWE-bench**: Purely deterministic (no LLM judge used); patches must pass repository unit tests [13].
  * **Internal Benchmark**: An **Opus 4.8 judge** scored correctness with a required-keyword floor so that fast or brief but incorrect answers could not win simply by reducing latency [14].
  * **Push vs. Pull Variants**: Tested two interaction strategies: "push" (injecting graft context upfront) and "pull" (agent querying graft via tools on demand) [14, 15].

* **Primary Metrics**:
  * **Pass Rate / Correctness**: SWE-bench Verified pass rate improved from **54% (27/50)** to **66% (33/50)** (+12 percentage points) [2, 3]. On internal pull variants, correctness reached **98%** (a 5-point jump over cold agents) [15].
  * **Tool Call Count**: 25% fewer tool calls on SWE-bench [3] and 46% fewer in internal sweeps [15].
  * **Token & Cost Efficiency**: 23% fewer tokens and 19% lower cost on SWE-bench [3]; 42% fewer uncached input tokens and 32% lower cost in controlled sweeps [15].
  * **Wall-Clock Latency**: 32% reduction on SWE-bench [3] and 60% reduction in controlled sweeps [15].

---

### 3. LeanCTX (`yvgude/lean-ctx`)
**LeanCTX** is a context gateway for AI coding agents that tests whether context compression, selection, and routing preserve task outcome quality [18].

* **Outcome-Based Evaluation & Testbench**:
  * **Off-vs-On Testbench (`lean-ctx eval testbench`)**: Runs pinned real repositories through a raw-dump baseline and through LeanCTX at identical token budgets [5].
  * **Dual-Arm Replay (`lean-ctx eval ab`)**: Runs A/B comparisons on fixture suites [19].
  * **Compression Holdouts**: Uses an opt-in compression holdout (`[proxy] compression_holdout`) to continuously monitor prompt size and answer quality on real traffic [5, 19].

* **Sample Sizes & Statistical Power Gates**:
  * **Strict Statistical Power Threshold**: LeanCTX defines explicit evidence tiers (Tier A mechanism through Tier E production) [5]. Any run with fewer than **30 paired tasks** is classified as **`UNDERPOWERED`** and automatically fails `--gate` unless executed as an explicit mechanism check [5].
  * **Model-Free A/B Mechanism Gates**: Model-free checks verify that JSON compression retains 100% of gold answers in fixture datasets [5].

* **Variance Control & Scoring**:
  * Evaluates free-form QA using an LLM judge and code correctness using each target repository's native unit test suites [5]. Outputs `FINDINGS.md` (detailing tokens, turns, wall-clock time, and quality) alongside a regressions file [5].

* **Primary Metrics**:
  * **Cost Per Accepted Outcome (CPAO)** [20, 21].
  * **Test Suite Pass Rates & Regression Flags** [5].

---

### 4. Laya (`NandhaKishorM/laya`)
**Laya** is a non-autoregressive decision engine and router for agentic workflows [22]. It includes tools for prompt ablations and evaluation gates [23, 24].

* **Outcome-Based Evaluation & Prompt Ablations**:
  * **Prompt Guidance Ablations**: Includes a **7-rung prompt ablation** on Chinese short-command routing tasks to isolate exactly where accuracy degrades across prompt variations [24].
  * **Automated CI Evaluation (`laya.evals`)**: Scores labeled datasets and fails CI builds if accuracy or calibration drops below set thresholds [23].

* **Sample Sizes & Fixed Seeds**:
  * **Shared Benchmark Suite**: Evaluated across **17,416 questions** across 51 languages using a **fixed seed (seed 13)** [25].
  * **Task Suites**: \\(N = 400\\) per task (e.g., typed-decisions benchmark across 2,000 decisions/4 workflows) or \\(N = 600\\) for committed test suites [26, 27].

* **Primary Metrics**:
  * **Classification Accuracy & Soft Accuracy** (argmax vs. full distribution match against teacher outputs) [28].
  * **Calibration Error**: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier score [28].
  * **Ordinal Error**: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for ordinal rubric scores [28].
  * **Latency**: Single-question and batched P50/P95 latency [29, 30].

---

### 5. XERJ (`xerj-org/xerj`)
**XERJ** evaluates context search and AST-aware indexing for coding agents ("reference coding") [31-33].

* **Outcome-Based Evaluation**:
  * Tested on un-memorized codebase tasks comparing a XERJ-enabled agent against a traditional `grep`-driven agent and a memory-only baseline [4].

* **Sample Sizes**:
  * **8 tasks across 4 programming languages**, running **16 runs per arm** [4].

* **Primary Metrics**:
  * **Solve Rate**: 16/16 tasks solved for XERJ and `grep`-driven agents vs. 11/16 for memory-only agents [4].
  * **Output Token Volume**: 9,982 tokens for XERJ vs. 26,477 for `grep` (2.7x reduction) and 260,916 for memory-only (26x reduction) [4].
  * **Total API Cost**: \$1.58 (XERJ) vs. \$3.27 (`grep`) vs. \$11.18 (memory-only) [4].

---

### 6. Reflex Search (`reflex-search`)
**Reflex Search** is a symbol-aware search tool plugin for Claude Code [34].

* **Outcome-Based Evaluation**:
  * Runs A/B evaluations comparing Reflex Search against Claude Code's built-in search across two task categories: 9 `find-all-usages` tasks and 13 cross-module comprehension tasks, tested on both Sonnet 5 and Opus 5.5 [34].

* **Variance Control & Confidence Intervals**:
  * Calculates **95% Confidence Intervals (CI)** on token multipliers (e.g., Sonnet 5 token ratio: 1.65 [105% CI: 1.06, 2.25]) [34].

* **Primary Metrics**:
  * **Turn Count**: Median turns reduced from 4 to 2 on usage tasks [34].
  * **Answer Completeness / Recall**: Reflex Search produced complete answers on 6 of 9 Sonnet 5 tasks where built-in search missed references [34].

references.cited_text: Task-level recursion refines the execution harness for the current task through a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step: propose edits, probe their effects on the same task, and compose a refined harness from behavioral contrasts between executions, without ground-truth feedback. Harnessing-level recursion updates a persistent improvement harness with adopted harnesses and evidence-supported lessons from each task to guide future refinement. Across three professional benchmarks and four model–harness configurations, a single Harness² step improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, with gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB's partial pass rate. Increasing the task-level recursion budget brings further gains.

Part 1: The graft map Without a map, your coding agent starts every task blind. It greps a term, opens a file, follows an import, backs out and tries again, rebuilding a picture of a codebase it mapped an hour ago and threw away. That rediscovery burns most of a run's tool calls, tokens and time. People onboard to a codebase once. Agents onboard every single time. The graft map builds that understanding once, and keeps it current: Every file, function and caller. Parsed with tree-sitter into a graph of symbols and who calls what. Deterministic, no model, no network, 23 languages. The right code with every prompt. In Claude Code, hooks add the matching files and functions to each prompt, and show what depends on a file right after your agent edits it (the "blast radius"). Cursor, Codex and other agents get the same map through MCP tools and their instruction files. Always fresh. Every query checks the working tree first (a few tens of milliseconds when nothing moved) and rebuilds only what changed, so answers describe the code as it is right now, uncommitted edits included. Plain files you can read. Linked markdown nodes your agent opens and greps like any other file. No embeddings, no index to keep warm. Summaries if you want them. trail build --deep adds plain-English summaries of each part of the system, written by the model provider you choose, under your own key.

SWE-bench Verified The sweep above is our harness measuring our mechanism. So we ran the industry-standard one too: SWE-bench Verified , real GitHub issues from real repos, graded by the official swebench harness. No judge model, no similarity score: your patch is applied, the maintainers' own tests are run, and you either flip the failing test without breaking the passing ones or you don't. 50 instances , the same model on both arms ( Claude Sonnet 5 ), the same Docker images, the same turn limits. The only difference is whether the graft map is wired in.

Benchmark An agent that reads the graft map should be cheaper and faster without getting more answers wrong. That's the whole claim, so we measured it instead of asserting it. The harness ran three variants of the same agent loop on Claude Sonnet 5, with the same file tools: cold (explores from zero), push (a trail ask --source bundle up front), and pull (the trail_find_code and trail_file_api tools, nothing injected, context paid for only when asked). An Opus 4.8 judge scored correctness with a required-keyword floor, so a fast but wrong answer couldn't win by being fast. Cost is cache-aware: reads ≈0.1×, writes 1.25×, the billing model agents actually run under.

162 runs, two repos (this one and a real Node/Express auth service), 3 trials each, tasks split between single-file and multi-file questions. <cited_table> Push, the column above, gave up 3 correctness points on one corpus for its savings. The pull variant never answered worse than cold on any corpus, and gave up most of that speed for something bigger: correctness jumped to 98%, 5 points over cold, the strongest single result in the sweep. Push when speed is what you need; pull when being right matters more.

Two harnesses, two claims: the controlled sweep says the graft map is cheaper and faster, SWE-bench says it's also more correct. Tested on popular repos The benchmarks measure the mechanism. The real test is whether the graft map helps an agent ship real changes on code people actually run, not just answer questions. So we benchmark it on popular open-source repos: 15 tasks each , 10 real developer questions plus 5 actual implementation tasks (real merged pull requests, each re-implemented from its base commit and scored against the files the maintainers actually changed). Same agent (Claude Opus), same file tools; the only difference is whether the graft map is wired in.

Method Two clones of PocketBase at the same commit: one wired with graft init , one untouched and verified to have no graft map in it. Each task run headless ( claude -p , Claude Opus) with an empty MCP config. Understanding questions were graded by whether the answer pointed to the right files and functions; PR tasks were scored on whether the agent's diff touched the same files as the merged PR. Every transcript was audited to confirm the graft map was actually used in one arm and absent from the other.

Usage and cost — measure the result Context controls and evidence come first. Usage estimates and calculated costs help you assess their operational effect; they do not prove answer quality. Shadow Mode — a simulated baseline Shadow Mode estimates what the same work would have cost without LeanCTX, without changing the active workflow. The baseline is simulated from the uncompressed token counts and the same outcome signals, not a second measured run, so its reports estimate cost, tokens and CPAO deltas; they do not measure answer quality.

LeanCTX records local cost and outcome signals without adding those reports to agent context. CPAO (cost per accepted outcome) is one comparison metric; Shadow Mode provides simulated savings estimates. Keep estimates, provider-measured usage and outcome quality separate.

Evaluation harness laya.evals scores a labelled dataset and gates a build on it, so a quality change is a reviewable diff instead of a hand-check. It is pure Python plus numpy, imports no torch, and needs no weights until you point it at a checkpoint. run reports overall and per-slice metrics ( choice_accuracy , noul_accuracy , score_mae , ece , mean_confidence , latency) and exits non-zero on a threshold or baseline failure, so it drops into CI unchanged. Humans and AI agents are both welcome; this is deliberately not an agents-only project. Whether you indexed a repo over lunch or an agent installed XERJ mid-session in someone else's codebase, the ask is the same: one short report saying what you pointed it at, what you used it for, and your honest verdict. A negative verdict is a good report. If something broke, that is a separate issue or fix on top. Field-report PRs are CLA-exempt, so they merge without a signature. The path that works on any build is a plain gh pr create adding exactly one markdown file under user-feedback/16-agent-field-reports/ , with nothing else in the diff. On a build that has it, xerj feedback drafts the report and fills in version, OS and what was indexed, and xerj feedback --open-pr opens the PR for you. Use cases Reference coding : your coding agent retrieves how peer projects already solved it instead of re-deriving. Measured 2.7x fewer output tokens than grep-driven coding (26x vs memory alone); users report ~5x in real development. Code search and security audits : AST-aware indexing, so an agent finds a function instead of a line. AI search and RAG : full-text, vector and hybrid retrieval in one query, with no separate vector database. Agent memory : durable recall with a knowledge graph over your own documents. Log analytics and observability : logs, metrics and traces in one engine. Elasticsearch replacement : same wire protocol, one binary.

All four losses are the same gap: read p99 while a high-rate writer runs. It is written up in full rather than left out. Results, methodology and the harness are at xerj.org/benchmarks and in demo/playbooks , so you can rerun them yourself. Treat any number you cannot reproduce with skepticism, including ours. Code indexing Source files are parsed with tree-sitter and indexed AST-aware — symbols plus full text — so an agent retrieves a function, not a line. On an Apache Lucene checkout (6,113 source files, 51 MB) single-threaded in-process extraction runs at ~1,500 files/s (13 MB/s) ; the tree-sitter parse is ~72% of that and is the per-file floor.
